narrative:
The model estimated a 68% probability that you would be a bad credit risk, so your loan application was denied. This does not mean you are certain to default; it means the information provided looked substantially riskier than what the model typically sees for approved applicants.

The strongest reason was your credit history. It was recorded as “all paid at bank,” which may sound positive, but only about 3% of approved applicants have this exact pattern, and it pushed the prediction most strongly toward bad credit. The second most important factor was your checking account status of 0–200 DM. A low balance in that range was less common among approved applicants than having no checking account, and it added to the risk assessment. Third, the purpose of the loan—a new car—also pushed toward bad credit; new-car loans were less common among approved applicants than radio/TV or furniture loans. Other details, such as requesting 15 months versus the approved average of about 19 months, were not enough to offset these concerns.

To improve your chances next time, ask the bank for the specific reasons on your file, check your credit report for errors, and focus on building a more consistent repayment record. Try to maintain a higher checking account balance before reapplying, and ask whether a co-signer, guarantor, or secured loan option could strengthen a future application.
